title: ‘Other Mommy’ Star Arabella Olivia Clark on Working With Jessica Chastain and Being Mentored by Mckenna Grace
description:
Arabella Olivia Clark is proud to scare you.

	The 10-year-old actress joined Variety over Zoom from her Los Angeles hotel room the morning after th
body:
Arabella Olivia Clark is proud to scare you.

	The 10-year-old actress joined Variety over Zoom from her Los Angeles hotel room the morning after the premiere of “Other Mommy, wearing a jacket with her character’s name, Bela, printed on the front. Clark plays the daughter of Ursula (Jessica Chastain) and Russ (Jay Duplass), a young girl terrorized by a sinister figure who looks just like her mother, known as the titular Other Mommy. 
	

	Released on Friday, the Rob Savage-directed film debuted at No. 1, earning $12.6 million domestically on its opening day. This is Clark’s first leading role, and she’s just getting started.


	For Clark, who previously played a younger version of Amanda Seyfried’s character in the 2025 film “The Housemaid,” “Other Mommy” marks her first time leading a feature film. Clark might specialize in frightening audiences, but she’s not easily frightened herself.

	“I love spiders. I love snakes. I like all the creepy stuff,” she replies when asked what scares her the most. “I love the dark, so I don’t really know what I would be afraid of.”

	Her mom, Rachel Clark, joins her off-camera in their L.A. hotel room, adding that nothing overtly frightening has ever held her back. “She’s always willing to try everything,” she says. “Even if she can’t do something, she’s like, ‘Yeah, I’ll try that.’”

	Clark’s open mind and adventurous spirit extend well beyond the screen. When she’s not acting, Clark takes sailing and swimming lessons — the latter of which came in handy for “Other Mommy” — and spends much of her free time reading. Before even landing the role of Bela, she read the film’s source material, Josh Malerman’s 2024 novel “Incidents Around the House,” in just three days. By her second audition, she was well prepared, though the story still managed to get under her skin. “I got chills!” she shares.
	

	But a few chills have never held her back. In fact, she’s a certified thrill-seeker at just 10 years old, even when it comes to her love for reading. Her favorite book is “Bunnicula,” a vampire rabbit set on a series of paranormal adventures, and she’s currently reading one of Jeff Kinney’s “Awesome Friendly Spooky Stories” books, which she proudly holds up to the camera. Combine that with her work on “Other Mommy” and “The Housemaid,” and she’s officially earned her status as a horror aficionado.

	Though she excels in the genre, she’s not quite ready to limit herself to it just yet. She aspires to venture into science fiction, particularly a potential sequel to “E.T.,” which would give her the chance to fulfill her dream of working with Steven Spielberg. Perhaps the film will also feature an appearance from yet another dream collaborator: Rocky, the beloved alien from “Project Hail Mary.”

	“Maybe Rocky and E.T. could be friends, because they’re both aliens, right?” Clark ponders.

	Whether she’s facing a terrifying doppelgänger, diving into a massive water tank or imagining supernova adventures, Clark is eager to try just about anything. Below, she discusses filming “Other Mommy,” learning from Chastain and her mentor-like relationship with former child actress Mckenna Grace.



	

					OTHER MOMMY, Arabella Olivia Clark, 2026. ph: Bernard Walsh /© Universal Pictures /Courtesy Everett Collection
									©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	“Other Mommy” scared me so bad! Were you scared while making it?

	Well, Rob Savage was always making sure I felt safe on set, and Jessica and Jay were always showing me different things and telling me different stories and making funny faces. 

	What was it like getting to work with Jessica Chastain? I know you mentioned you had a lot of fun together behind the scenes.

	Working with Jessica Chastain was a great experience. I spent time with her and her kids, and she’s a great mom. We were always going to the park and hiking and all that stuff. One time — well, a bunch of times — I was in her trailer, and she was also studying for Harvard. And I can’t believe it! She’s a mom, and also studying for Harvard and also filming a movie at the same time. I learned a lot from her.

	What was one of your favorite memories that you have from being on set for “Other Mommy”?
	

	One of my favorite memories is when Jessica did her witch cackle. She’s like, “OK everybody, it’s going to be loud.” And she did it, and I was so surprised. She could be a witch in a movie.

	That part scared me! How did it not freak you out?

	Well, once the camera’s rolling, it’s one thing. But when it’s not rolling, they’re all telling funny jokes or telling funny stories or showing me different pictures. Or taking pictures with me.

	You were also in “The Housemaid,” which had me scared too. Do you love doing scary stuff?

	I really do. Paul Feig was amazing. I played a young role of Amanda Seyfried, and I’m always gonna look up to her. 

	What is your favorite movie that Amanda’s done? I think my favorite is probably “Mamma Mia.”

	That’s my favorite! And “Mean Girls.”

	There’s a part in the movie where you play Other Bela, an evil version of your character. Which version was more fun to play?

	Other Bela!

	You should play a bad guy in your next horror movie.

	Okay! I also want to do sci-fi. Like sharks and stuff. I like experiencing the stuff that’s not actually real. I want to go to space and then have aliens and octopuses and sharks in the movie. Like a whole sci-fi movie combined!

	What’s your favorite sci-fi movie?

	I love “The Meg.” And “Project Hail Mary,” the new one that just came out. I love Rocky! I want my own Rocky. I love science and doing all different projects and space. I would love to be in space. And I love reading spooky stories in the dark with a flashlight at night.

	You’re only 10, and I still get scared at 23. You’re braver than I am! 

	Thank you! I love doing all the stunts. I got to do different flips and spins, and I love doing acrobatics. And I love the water scenes too, because I got to swim a lot, and that’s one of my hobbies. Swimming and sailing.

	How did you film that scene in the water?

	Arabella: It was a big, big pool. It was massive. It was a big tank that was, like, 20 feet down?

	Rachel: It was 20 feet down. Watching her film in the water was one of the scariest moments as a mom, because the tank was pitch black. There were balls. She had that Sherpa hoodie on, pulling her down, and they had the pyrotechnic people where there was an explosion in the water. And they had to yank her underwater. The timing and everything was so well orchestrated. But of course, as a mom, it was very anxiety-producing.
	

	Arabella: It was fun. I love swimming, and I love being in deep pools. I can dive down all the way to 10 feet!

	Do you know who Mckenna Grace is?Yes!

	Well, you remind me so much of her. I was just talking about how I think you’re going to have the same career as her!

	Rachel: Do you want to know something? Mckenna Grace is so sweet. She reached out to Arabella and offered to mentor her and be there for her to talk about things like growing up in the industry.

	Arabella: We only talked online. But I’m hoping to meet her in person!

schema.headline: ‘Other Mommy’ Star Arabella Olivia Clark on Working With Jessica Chastain and Being Mentored by Mckenna Grace

title: New ‘Naruto’ Anime Series and ‘Shadow Rising’ Manga Revealed
description: Big news for “Naruto” fans: the franchise is getting a new anime TV series and author Masashi Kishimoto is releasing another “Naruto” manga titled “
body:
Big news for “Naruto” fans: the franchise is getting a new anime TV series and author Masashi Kishimoto is releasing another “Naruto” manga titled “Shadow Rising.”

	The new anime series will be a crossover with the popular manga “NINKŪ” and will be supervised by both Kishimoto and “NINKŪ” creator Koji Kiriyama.

	Per the description for the upcoming “NARUTOxNINKŪ” anime, “Team 7 members Naruto, Sasuke, and Sakura are given a mission by Kakashi. Since Kakashi cannot participate himself, Naruto is appointed acting leader. As a result of this decision, Naruto is fully motivated to make the mission a success. However, on the way, Team 7 finds themselves lost in another world. What appears before the bewildered trio is a boy with a face resembling a frog’s, named Fūsuke. What awaits them in this strange new world?”
	

	The news was announced Saturday during a “Naruto” panel at New York Comic Con, which concluded with the unveiling of new “Naruto” manga, “Shadow Rising.” That reveal came at the very end of the panel in a teaser video that noted more details will be shared during Jump Festa 2027 in December.


	Also during the panel, a message from “Naruto” live-action movie director Destin Daniel Cretton was shared that teases more about the upcoming film.

	“When we kicked off our worldwide search for Team 7 this summer, I talked about what an honor it is to bring Kishimoto-sensei’s incredible world and characters to life,” Cretton wrote. “The further we get into making this film, the more excited I am about what we’re creating. What I’ve always loved about Naruto is that he’s the character who might normally get sidelined as a sidekick. He’s excitable, he tries too hard, and people underestimate him. But he has an incredible heart. No matter how many times he fails or gets knocked down, he never stops believing in himself or fighting for the people he loves. That spirit is at the heart of the story we’re telling. These characters mean so much to so many people, myself included, and I carry that with me as we make this film. We’re approaching the world, relationships, and journeys Kishimoto-sensei created with a lot of care, and we want to capture what makes ‘Naruto’ so special. We’re hard at work and will have more to share soon. Until then, thank you for your passion, your patience, and for being along for the ride. I can’t wait for you to see what’s ahead!”
	

	Watch the teaser for the upcoming “NARUTOxNINKŪ” anime and new manga “Shadow Rising” in the videos below.

schema.headline: New ‘Naruto’ Anime Series and ‘Shadow Rising’ Manga Revealed

title: ‘The Furious’ Star Xie Miao to Headline U.S.-Set Martial Arts Crime Thriller for Stars Collective (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Chinese martial arts star Xie Miao (“The Furious,” the “Eye for an Eye” series) is set to lead an English-language action crime thriller set in the
body:
Chinese martial arts star Xie Miao (“The Furious,” the “Eye for an Eye” series) is set to lead an English-language action crime thriller set in the U.S., which Los Angeles-based Stars Collective has in development.

	The project will pursue the bruising, realistic style of martial arts action seen in “The Furious,” and is designed to appeal to genre fans while building Xie’s standing as an international action lead.


	Peter Luo (“Malignant,” “Umma,” “The Garfield Movie”), Wayne Wei Jiang (“The Meg”) and Wei Junzi (“Eye for an Eye,” “The Furious”) are producing. Stars Collective co-CEO Nancy Xu (“The Rip,” “The Monkey,” “The Garfield Movie”) produces for the company.
	

	“Xie Miao is the perfect artist to lead this fast-paced, adrenaline-fueled movie, with real physical requirements only a professional of his caliber can perform,” said Xu.

	Born in Beijing, Xie started out as a child actor and collected multiple wushu championship titles. He broke through opposite Jet Li, with the pair cast as father and son in “The New Legend of Shaolin” and “My Father Is a Hero.”

	Alongside a film career spanning decades, Xie, who holds a degree in ethnic sports, also worked on martial arts television shows. His screen work eventually landed him the lead in the “Eye for an Eye” franchise. Most recently, he headlined the action hit “The Furious.”

	“Xie Miao is a powerful and distinctive action star. ‘The Furious’ showcased his appeal in hard-hitting action, and this new project will broaden the scope of the story and give his character more room, letting audiences around the world see even more of what he can do,” said Wei.
	

	Jiang said the film would hold on to the strongest elements of classic martial arts cinema while taking a more global approach to its storytelling and production. “We hope to make an action film that transcends language and geography and resonates with audiences everywhere,” he said.

	The news was unveiled on the sidelines of the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market.

	Stars Collective has been chasing rights deals to fill out its global film slate. The company recently picked up Mandarin-language remake rights to “Thelma,” the 2024 Sundance breakout that became Magnolia Pictures’ top-grossing release ever, and has begun developing a feature with the working title “Grandma, Please.”

	It has also optioned the nonfiction book “Fortunate Sons: The 120 Chinese Boys Who Came to America, Went to School, and Revolutionized an Ancient Civilization,” which it is adapting for the screen with Oscar winner Donna Gigliotti (“Silver Linings Playbook,” “Hidden Figures,” “Shakespeare in Love”).

	Launched in 2020, Stars Collective is based in Los Angeles and runs operations in China and Japan. Its slate of more than 60 original properties in development stretches from film and animation to games, merchandise and immersive experiences.

	Its incubator is anchored by 15 industry mentors, among them directors Sam Raimi, Jon M. Chu, Alan Taylor and Lu Chuan, screenwriter Anthony McCarten, actor-producer Huang Xiaoming and producers including Gigliotti, Paula Wagner, Patrick Wachsberger and Rob Minkoff. The company counts over 320 filmmakers and artists, drawn from 45 countries, among its members.

schema.headline: ‘The Furious’ Star Xie Miao to Headline U.S.-Set Martial Arts Crime Thriller for Stars Collective (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Ibuku’ Review: Dreamlike Indonesian Drama Is a Compelling Tale of Parental Redemption
description: The fraught relationship between an estranged mother and daughter takes centre stage in “Ibuku,” the fourth film from Indonesian writer-director Edd
body:
The fraught relationship between an estranged mother and daughter takes centre stage in “Ibuku,” the fourth film from Indonesian writer-director Eddie Cahyono. Despite the first-person perspective of the title — which translates as “my mother” in Indonesian — most of the film is seen through the eyes of Sumiati (Christine Hakim), a mother and recent widow struggling to gather money to visit her daughter Sri (Ayushita Nugraha) in a Saudi prison. Much of the film’s emotional burden, as well as its photography, lands on the face of Hakim, captured through still, observational camerawork as she enacts various rituals of cooking, gathering, dancing, even spelunking, all shaded by grief for the impending loss of her daughter, and her responsibility in driving her away from home. 
	

	Premiering in Competition at the Busan Film Festival, Cahyono’s film is most compelling when its spiritual qualities are felt rather than seen, when its story is discovered through Hakim’s layered and complex performance. The filmmaker has spoken about his personal connection to the material, which is informed by his own experience of leaving the village for a better life, to send money home. Not that this is autofiction: “Ibuku” finds its basis in the contemporary exploitation of migrant workers, and traces the tragedies of this demographic back to their roots at home.


	Though “Ibuku” is mostly seen through Sumiati’s eyes, it opens with the perspective of her daughter Sri. Projections of Sumiati surround her in a sort of cage, as Sri proclaims that she wishes she could hate her mother — complex feelings that stem from a feeling of abandonment to her abusive arranged marriage. When the film next cuts back to this room, Sri explains that this is the root of her decision to leave and work in Saudi Arabia. This context of parental failure looms over the rest of “Ibuku,” with Sumiati’s every action haunted by her regret over not protecting her daughter from abusers both at home and abroad.
	

	The next time we hear from Sri is years later, as Sumiati discovers her daughter has been sentenced to death for killing her employer and would-be rapist. Given her late husband’s gambling debts, she doesn’t have the means to visit, and instead must borrow money from her fellow villagers to attempt to see her daughter. The misery of the situation could feel overwhelming, even cruel, but Cahyono’s observation of Sumiati’s struggles is humane and sympathetic. He’s interested in the relationship between different societal pressures and patriarchal exploitations, but also in Sumiati’s own regretful culpability in these practices: Sri’s arranged marriage was a desperate play on her mother’s part to get out of debt through dowry.

	Sumiati is a once-famous performer of Jathilian, a form of Javanese dance (also known as Kuda Lumping) in which the performers are “possessed,” the ritual accompanied by a shaman as well as percussion. Such spiritual communion extends to Cahyono’s intimate handheld cinematography, which, when not centered on Hakim, frames her home and landmarks in the village as though Sri and her husband are still present, the grainy and dreamlike haze of film making that connection feel ever-present.

	The locations are often stunning, notably the deep-nested roots of a tree extending into a cave where Sumiati goes spelunking for water and later attempts to build functioning pipework. The water is shot with an orange glow, and the image carries a spiritual power that continues through the film’s capturing of Hakim’s sensitive and mournful performance — as Sumiati subtly entreats forgiveness from the spectres of her departed family, and in turn from the village. The village itself is represented through the kindly but put-upon figure of the chief Djatmiko (Landung Simatupang), who himself must reckon with potential transgressions between himself and Sumiati.

	The effect dissipates somewhat whenever Cahyono resorts to less suggestive, more blatantly surreal imagery. In one moment, the spectre of Sumiati’s deceased husband watches silently over the tree from which he once hanged himself; in another, more delirious instance, Sumiati is suspended in the air by invisible wires after she joins in a dance performance without permission. At least there’s no further elaboration beyond these flourishes, which feel indelicate by the film’s standards. The striking opening, with its setup of Sri silhouetted against filmed images of her mother’s dance, already demonstrates the impossible communicative power of the visual artform. Audiences don’t need more help getting the message.

schema.headline: ‘Ibuku’ Review: Dreamlike Indonesian Drama Is a Compelling Tale of Parental Redemption

title: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Says A.I. Is Being Trained to ‘Hijack Your Intimacy’: ‘We Should Be Concerned’
description: Joseph Gordon-Levitt, who has added United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance to his resumé, has warned the public to be “
body:
Joseph Gordon-Levitt, who has added United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance to his resumé, has warned the public to be “concerned about the people building A.I.” and how the technology is being trained to “hijack your intimacy” in a vlog-style video interview with The New York Times published on Saturday.

	When the outlet asked what he fears most about AI, the “500 Days of Summer” actor said he doesn’t want to reduce “these concerns into one sound bite of fear.” “That’s one of the problems. To me, saying: Oh, I’m scared that A.I. could exterminate all of humanity — that doesn’t really get at the substance of the concern. There’s real validity to that concern. But that’s not the thing that really worries me,” Gordon-Levitt said.
	

	He continued, saying what worries him is the “decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy.” “These companies are betting on the notion that they’re going to take over the entire economy. That would be totalitarianism, and that would be really bad… Simultaneously, these models are being trained to hijack your intimacy, to make friends with you, to get you to fall in love with it. We shouldn’t be scared of an A.I. We should be concerned about the people building A.I.”


	Gordon-Levitt was appointed to a brand-new United Nations position in March. At the time, the organization defined it as “a newly established role designed to strengthen public understanding of how digital technologies shape everyday life, rights and opportunities.” 

	The actor and director has long been outspoken about A.I., and in January, joined more than 700 artists, writers and creators, including Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, in supporting an anti-AI campaign calling out tech companies exploiting copyrighted work without permission.
	

	Watch the full video here.

schema.headline: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Says A.I. Is Being Trained to ‘Hijack Your Intimacy’: ‘We Should Be Concerned’

title: Matthew Lillard Says He Thought ‘Scream’ Was ‘Lame’ and ‘Nobody’ Would See the Movie Before It Became a Hit: ‘Here We Are 30 Years Later’
description: Matthew Lillard might best be known for his appearances throughout the uber-popular “Scream” franchise, but when he filmed the original installment,
body:
Matthew Lillard might best be known for his appearances throughout the uber-popular “Scream” franchise, but when he filmed the original installment, he didn’t think it would become the cult classic its regarded as today.

	“I was in the back of a car, driving home from work one night, at like six in the morning, covered in blood,” Lillard said during a panel at New York Comic Con (via EW). He explained that he and his co-stars were discussing their next career moves: Courtney Cox was returning to “Friends,” while Neve Campbell was going back to “Party of Five.” “And I’d literally just been on a pilot, and I’m like, ‘This movie’s lame. Nobody’s gonna see it. I’m going to go become a television star,’” said Lillard.
	

	He continued to say “that pilot never went, and here we are 30 years later,” adding “nobody could have possibly ever imagined” what “Scream” would become. The first film, released in 1996, began a seven-film franchise, with the latest installment having been released earlier this year.


	Lillard played one of the original Ghostface killers, Stuart “Stu” Macher, in the film. In addition to Cox and Campbell, he starred alongside Skeet Ulrich, David Arquette, Drew Barrymore and others.

	Recently, Lillard got honest about his feelings toward another franchise he starred in: the early 2000s live-action “Scooby-Doo” and “Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed.” While participating in Variety‘s “Know Their Lines” video series, the “She’s All That” actor admitted he began to resent the films after the latter disappointed at the box office.
	

	“It was the first big movie that I was in and it was a big opportunity for me,” he said. “And then I felt that ‘Scooby Doo’ is this big movie, I’m now going to go off and be a big movie star. And it was right about this time, after the second movie, that my career took a real nosedive for a long time. Like, I may be one of those guys from the ’90s that never comes back. This movie is a love-hate relationship for me because I was like, ‘It’s “Scooby Doo’s” fault. That’s why I’m not working.’”

schema.headline: Matthew Lillard Says He Thought ‘Scream’ Was ‘Lame’ and ‘Nobody’ Would See the Movie Before It Became a Hit: ‘Here We Are 30 Years Later’

title: ‘Tenzing’ Review: A Remarkable Adventure That Puts the Audience Right Up on Mount Everest, Along with the First Two Men — One a Sherpa, Overlooked by History — to Scale It
description: The movies are having a mountain-climbing moment. More than a moment, really — it’s been building since 2018, the year that saw the release of not o
body:
The movies are having a mountain-climbing moment. More than a moment, really — it’s been building since 2018, the year that saw the release of not one but two jaw-dropping, vertigo-inducing, heart-in-the-throat documentaries, “Free Solo” and “The Dawn Wall,” that took you right up to the places that climbers crave and that most of us wouldn’t dare to go near. But as these films demonstrate, we might well dream of it. The new mountaineering movies are delirious vicarious cinema, employing technological means and a filmmaking bravado that comes with them that would have been unimaginable three or four decades ago. Movies like “14 Peaks” and “The Alpinist” — or “Skywalkers: A Love Story,” the great documentary about rooftoppers — chart the impossible, and the very fact that the films exist can seem part of the impossible. That’s an element of their scary exhilaration.
	

	“Tenzing” fits into the genre, though in a far more traditional way. It’s not a documentary. It’s a drama, and a rather old-school one: the story of the first climb to reach the peak of Mount Everest, which happened in 1953. It’s a tale of courage, ambition, arrogance, death, and triumph, and it’s also a story of embattled national pride and ethnic identity. The team that scaled Everest in 1953 was led by the British, who were in the last throes of trying to stake out their empire. No one had ever made it to the top of Mount Everest (there had been eight previous attempts), and this team barely did either. The elements were too forbidding: the chasms and vertical rock faces, the wind and the storms, and the air — so thin it could kill you. The Brits were ready to conquer, but they couldn’t have made the climb without their team of Sherpa, the Tibetan ethnic group native to the area, who had mountaineering in their blood. The Sherpa were officially the “guides,” but they knew what they were doing far more than the British did.
	

	On that revolutionary trek, the first two people to reach the summit of Everest were Edmund Hillary, who was a New Zealander, and Tenzing Norgay, a Nepalese-Indian Sherpa who’d been dreaming of scaling Everest ever since he was a boy. These two were the Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin of mountaineering. But for decades, because of his ethnicity, Tenzing’s role in the mission was understated by history; he was treated as Hillary’s noble assistant. “Tenzing” celebrates his rightful place as a mountaineering visionary — and it does so by dramatizing this climb with a filmmaking rigor that’s stately and inviting and, at moments, ominous and casually miraculous. (When a vast plain of snow suddenly collapses, you feel like a hole just opened up in the earth.) “Tenzing” earns its inspirational fervor, but the reason it fits into the new wave of mountain-climbing movies is that the director, Jennifer Peedom, an Australian who’s been making documentaries about mountain-climbing for 18 years, has staged it with a you-are-there authenticity that’s breathtaking but never showy. She’s a classicist; this is a movie that, in spirit, you could imagine John Huston or Howard Hawks having directed.

	The film opens with Tenzing as a boy, gawking at Mount Everest, which looms across the valley like Godzilla. It sits on the border of Nepal and China in the Himalayas, and Tenzing grows up in the shadow of its awe. He calls the mountain by its Tibetan name, Chomolungma, and early on has an encounter with the legendary British alpinist George Mallory (Johnny Flynn), who was part of the first three Everest expeditions in the 1920s. So from the start, the spirit of this endeavor will be global.

	Peedom isn’t just a filmmaking wizard. She’s a humanist who dramatizes the intricate politics of the 1953 Everest climb, which was led by John Hunt, a British colonel (played with stiff-upper-lip exuberance by Willem Dafoe) who believes that the entire mission should be run in a strict military manner. He’s right in certain ways, but the trouble is that his outlook prioritizes hierarchy, which places the Sherpa at the bottom of the pecking order.

	The film flashes back, maybe a little too much, to key periods of Tenzing’s life (his boyhood, his meeting of the woman he’ll marry). But it’s most interesting when he has to fight and cajole his way onto the expedition. Genden Phunstok, the Chinese actor of Tibetan descent who plays Tenzing, is disarmingly handsome, and in his quiet way he’s a star. Dealing with the British, his Tenzing is scrupulous and honorable, but don’t confuse that with subservience. He’s got a will of iron, and a velvet wit, and something else the British don’t have: a faith in the power of Everest that allows him to see the mountain as an ally rather than an adversary. He’s not trying to conquer the mountain; he’s trying to fuse with it. That gives him a whole different outlook as a climber.
	

	As the mission goes on, Tenzing forms a connection with Edmund Hillary, played with frosty empathetic reserve by Tom Hiddleston. The two men have much in common; they are fearless but modest. “Tenzing” captures the sometimes prickly camaraderie of the team members, a drama that feeds into the logistics of the climb, which the movie dramatizes with a stunning existential flair. You literally watch “Tenzing” and think, “How on earth did they film this?” It’s the living definition of an adventure movie, but without adventure-movie corniness. The film never overhypes the danger or the dread, and it cuts no dramatic corners. It knows that the real story is gripping enough.

	As the men draw closer to the peak, the likelihood of reaching it actually grows more distant. The weather is too forbidding; the window of time gets smaller. Tenzing is promoted to being an official team member, and when he and Hillary are finally tapped as the two who will make the last leg of the trek, that’s because it’s now clear that they’re the only two who can do it. Even then, their triumph is far from assured; the climb becomes more unreal in its harshness. The pull of “Tenzing” is that we in the audience are there, right along with them, every snowy, icy, impossible step of the way.

schema.headline: ‘Tenzing’ Review: A Remarkable Adventure That Puts the Audience Right Up on Mount Everest, Along with the First Two Men — One a Sherpa, Overlooked by History — to Scale It

title: ‘Project Hail Mary’ Composer Daniel Pemberton, ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Songwriter EJAE Triumph at World Soundtrack Awards
description: Daniel Pemberton was named Film Composer of the Year at the World Soundtrack Awards on Saturday, capping a prolific run that includes “Project Hail
body:
Daniel Pemberton was named Film Composer of the Year at the World Soundtrack Awards on Saturday, capping a prolific run that includes “Project Hail Mary,” “The Drama,” “The Bad Guys 2” and “Masters of the Universe.” The British composer has now won three times at the Ghent-based ceremony, taking the top prize in 2021 and Discovery of the Year in 2014. 

	For “Project Hail Mary,” Pemberton mined the unfamiliar for universal resonance, experimenting with wood, metal and glass and even drawing inspiration from a friend’s leaky faucet. “It was a case of throwing every crazy idea we could into the score, but at the same time, it had to be really emotional,” he said at a roundtable shortly before the closing ceremony. “I spent a lot of time trying to make people cry.” 
	

	Fresh off their Academy Award win, pop star EJAE and songwriter Mark Sonnenblick took Best Original Song for the “KPop Demon Hunters” chart-topper “Golden.” The win adds to a haul that includes a Golden Globe, a Grammy and a David Guetta remix. The winners, however, were not on hand to collect. 


	Speaking to Variety last year, EJAE pushed back against labels. “As an artist, I don’t want myself to be boxed into being a ‘K-pop’ artist because I don’t really view myself as a K-pop artist or a pop artist,” she said. “I view myself as a songwriter of every genre.”

	Among the night’s other honorees, Jeff Russo won Television Composer of the Year for “Alien: Earth,” “Cape Fear” and “Citadel”; Kevin Smithers took the Public Choice Award for the Mexican stop-motion feature “Soy Frankelda”; and Northern Irish composer Hannah Peel (“Midwinter Break”) won Discovery of the Year. 
	

	Smithers is developing a new, musical stop-motion feature with “Frankelda” directors Arturo and Roy Ambriz, while Peel is now scoring Netflix’s series adaptation of “Assassin’s Creed.”

	Russo’s music for “Cape Fear” and “Alien: Earth” both emphasized dread — all while drawing on the legacies of Bernard Herrmann, James Horner and Jerry Goldsmith. In “Cape Fear,” for instance, Russo incorporated themes from Herrmann’s original 1962 score.

	“That made my job both easier and much harder,” Russo said. “I had to figure out how Herrmann writes harmonically so the two scores could sound sympathetic and live together.” 

	On “Alien: Earth,” he drew on the contrasting approaches of Goldsmith, who played up dread in “Alien,” and Horner, whose “Aliens” music leaned toward militarism and action. Russo looked more for inspiration, lifting few specific themes, save for a delayed horn motif from Goldsmith’s original. “I thought it was fun [for franchise aficionados to recognize the easter egg]. We’re all here to have fun, right?”

	Conductor Dirk Brossé and the Brussels Philharmonic  certainly did — enlivening the closing gala with performances of selected music by guest of honor Hildur Guðnadóttir and lifetime achievement award recipient Trevor Jones, both of whom were on hand for the show.

	The program included themes from “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” “Tár,” “Joker,” “The Dark Crystal,” “The Last of the Mohicans” and “Notting Hill.” At one point, Guðnadóttir even grabbed her cello to accompany the orchestra onstage.



	

									Courtesy of Ben Croll
	



	Full list of winners below: 

	Film Composer of the Year:Daniel Pemberton – “Project Hail Mary,” “The Drama,” “The Bad Guys 2,” “Masters of the Universe”

	Television Composer of the Year:Jeff Russo – “Alien: Earth,” “Cape Fear,” “Citadel” (Season 2)

	Best Original Song:“Golden” from “KPop Demon Hunters” – written by Kim Eun-jae, Mark Sonnenblick, Joong Gyu Kwak, Yu Han Lee, Hee Dong Nam, Jeong Hoon Seo, Teddy Park; performed by Huntrix

	Discovery of the Year:Hannah Peel – “Midwinter Break”

	Public Choice Award:Kevin Smithers – “Soy Frankelda”

	Game Music Award:Nicolas Garcia – “Cthulhu: The Cosmic Abyss”
	

	Belgian Film Composer of the Year (Powered by Sabam):Margaret Hermant – “A La Cara: Mallorca Confidencial”

	Award for the Best Original Composition by a Young Composer (Powered by Vienna Synchron Stage):Xabier Doural García

	Lifetime Achievement Award:Trevor Jones

title: ‘Star Trek: Starfleet Academy’ Season 2 Adds Bill Nighy, Rosemarie DeWitt in Guest Roles
description:
Bill Nighy and Rosemarie DeWitt are set to guest star in “Star Trek: Starfleet Academy” Season 2. 

	The announcement was revealed during the “Star
body:
Bill Nighy and Rosemarie DeWitt are set to guest star in “Star Trek: Starfleet Academy” Season 2. 

	The announcement was revealed during the “Star Trek” panel at New York Comic-Con on Saturday. Nighy will play Nahla’s (Holly Hunter) estranged father, Nyk Ake, while DeWitt will play Tarima’s (Zoë Steiner) mother, Laytha Sadal, the First Lady of Betazed.

	First-look photos of the two new guest stars can be seen below. 


	The panelists for “Starfleet Academy” included Hunter, Sandro Rosta, Bella Shepard, Karim Diané, Robert Picardo and co-showrunners and executive producers Alex Kurtzman and Noga Landau. An exact premiere date is yet to be set, but the second season of the show will launch in March 2027 on Paramount+. 
	

	As Variety exclusively reported in March, Season 2 will be the show’s final season. The logline for “Starfleet Academy” Season 2 states that it “follows our cadets into their second year aboard the USS Athena. There, their ideals of leadership, friendship, romance and morality are put to the test as they navigate budding rivalries, shaky diplomatic negotiations, a fiercely competitive schoolwide tournament, and the arrival of a mysterious new cadet whose existence raises questions that could have consequences far beyond the classroom.”



	

					L-R: Robert Picardo as The Doctor and Bill Nighy as Nyk in season 2 of Star Trek: Starfleet Academy streaming on Paramount+. Photo Credit: Michael Gibson/Paramount+
									Michael Gibson/Paramount+
	





	

					L-R: Zoë Steiner as Tarima and Rosemarie DeWitt as Laytha Sadal in season 2 of Star Trek: Starfleet Academy streaming on Paramount+. Photo Credit: Michael Gibson/Paramount+

title: Christa Pike Released From Hospital After Surviving Botched Execution
description:
Christa Pike
                          Released From Hospital
                          ... Back
body:
Christa Pike
                          Released From Hospital
                          ... Back Behind Bars
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 10, 2026
                            8:41 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 10, 2026
                                9:31 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate who survived a botched lethal injection last month, is out of the hospital and back behind bars.
      
    
            The 50-year-old convicted killer was discharged from the hospital and returned to the women's prison where she's spent the past 30 years.
      
    
            Pike's attorneys confirmed the news Saturday, saying she's still receiving medical attention following the failed execution.
      

            In a statement, her attorneys said Pike is thankful for the first responders and medical professionals who treated her, adding they're continuing to monitor her recovery.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... Pike was scheduled to be executed September 30 for the brutal 1995 murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer.
      
    
            However, the execution went horribly wrong when Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital, the drug Tennessee uses for lethal injections.
      
    
            Instead of being pronounced dead, Pike was transported to a hospital for emergency medical care ... where she remained until her release.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The failed execution has since raised serious questions about Tennessee's lethal injection procedures.
      
    
            A judge also ordered the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve all evidence connected to Pike's botched execution.
      
    
            Pike was sentenced to death for the murder of Slemmer, who was beaten and stabbed to death in 1995.

description:

body:
UFC Star Tim Kennedy
                          Reportedly Shot Multiple Times During Congo Ambush
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 10, 2026
                            12:37 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Tim Kennedy -- a former star in the UFC -- has reportedly been shot multiple times while working with a private military contractor in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
      
    
            The Vectus Group -- a PMC owned by Erik Prince, the co-founder of the now-defunct Blackwater -- suffered serious casualties earlier this week while assisting Congo's army.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Twenty people were killed or injured ... including Kennedy, who is reportedly receiving medical treatment at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Washington, D.C. The Daily Mail reports he was shot multiple times in the leg, but he's expected to survive.
      

            At least Congolese people and a former New Zealand special forces soldier were killed during the attack.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The Daily Mail reports this is the PMC's first fatality in Congo. A spokesperson for Vectus declined to comment on the attack when asked by the outlet.
      
    
            Tim Kennedy compiled an MMA record of 18-6 during a 15-year career. He fought in UFC, WEC, Strikeforce, and several other competitions. Kennedy joined the U.S. Army back in 2004 ... before transitioning from active duty to the Texas Army National Guard in 2009.
